title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 29: Velez v. De Vera: Succession to the IBP Presidency
primary_topics: Chapter 29 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a digest of Velez v. De Vera, decided per curiam, in which the Court suspended Atty. Leonard de Vera for two years for the unauthorized use of a client's funds and upheld his removal from the IBP board and the election of his successor as executive vice-president.

The ethics holding: a foreign suspension order transmutes into a Philippine one only if the foreign court's basis included a ground for discipline here, and depositing a client's $12,000 check in one's own account and using it is malpractice, gross misconduct and unethical behavior -- though suspension, not disbarment, was the fitting penalty.

The due process holding: the position of IBP executive vice-president is not property in the constitutional sense and carries no security of tenure, and in administrative proceedings the essence of due process is simply the opportunity to explain one's side.

The governance holding: the rotation rule attaches to the office of executive vice-president while the presidency passes by automatic succession, so the replacement EVP had to come from the incumbent board -- making the elections of Governors Santiago and then Salazar valid.
sub_topics: In AC No. 6697 complainant Zoilo Antonio Velez sought the suspension or disbarment of Atty. Leonard de Vera for concealing a suspension order rendered against him by the State Bar of California and for violating the rotation rule of Administrative Matter No. 491.

The California matter arose from an insurance case for Julius Wills III, injured in a 1986 automobile accident: de Vera received a $12,000 settlement check on his client's behalf and deposited it in his personal account, for which a hearing referee recommended a three-year suspension; the case was never decided on the merits because he resigned from the California Bar.

On the rotation ground, the complainant alleged that de Vera's transfer of membership from the PPLM chapter to the Agusan del Sur chapter -- where he neither resided nor held office -- was a circumvention made solely to become IBP national president.

Two companion matters were consolidated: Bar Matter No. 1227, de Vera's request that the Court schedule his oath-taking as IBP national president, and AM No. 05-5-15-SC, the letter-report of National President Jose Anselmo I. Cadiz on the IBP Resolution removing him for acts inimical to the board and the IBP.

The dispute began when the IBP board approved the withdrawal of its Petition in Integrated Bar of the Philippines et al. v. Senate of the Philippines et al., after which de Vera allegedly made untruthful statements, innuendos and blatant lies about that Resolution during the plenary session of the 10th National IBP Convention.

Governor Romulo A. Rivera wrote on May 12, 2005 seeking his removal, and the next day the board resolved by a two-thirds vote to remove him as board member and executive vice-president; Governor Pura Angelica Y. Santiago was elected EVP on June 13, relinquished the post on June 20, and Governor Jose Vicente B. Salazar was elected in her stead on June 25.

President Cadiz then asked the Court to approve Salazar's election and assumption as national president should de Vera be disbarred or suspended or his removal approved, while de Vera protested both elections and claimed he had been removed without notice or due process.

On the first issue, the Court unanimously held that AC No. 6052 was no bar to AC No. 6697: the earlier case concerned his qualification to run for governor for Eastern Mindanao under the IBP bylaws, the present one his privilege to practice law under the Lawyer's Oath and the Code of Professional Responsibility, and the two sought different relief.

On the second issue, citing Maquera, the Court held that a foreign judgment of suspension transmutes into a Philippine one only if its basis included a ground for disbarment or suspension here, and that by insisting he was authorized by his client's father to use the funds, de Vera impliedly admitted using them for himself.

Canon 16 being emphatic on the point, holding a client's money without acquiescence was indicative of lack of integrity and propriety, and depositing the check in his own account made him guilty of malpractice, gross misconduct and unethical behavior in violation of his oath of fidelity to his client.
Because disbarment should not be decreed where a lesser penalty would accomplish the end desired, and considering the amount involved, the Court imposed suspension for two years.

The transfer of chapter membership, however, was within his rights: neither the Code nor the Lawyer's Oath punishes a lawyer for aspiring to the IBP presidency or forbids perfectly legal acts to accomplish that goal.

On the third issue, the Court held that the EVP position is not property in the constitutional sense and carries no security of tenure, removal for cause requiring only a resolution of two thirds of the remaining board members.

Due process was satisfied: in administrative proceedings its essence is the opportunity to explain one's side, cross-examination is not indispensable and an actual hearing is not always essential; de Vera received a copy of the Complaint, was present at the meeting, and the transcript showed he had a fair opportunity to answer Atty. Rivera's accusations.

The arithmetic also held: 'remaining members' excluded the complainant and the respondent, and of the seven qualified to vote, five voted for expulsion and two against, satisfying the two-thirds requirement.

On removal for cause, the Court observed that conflicts are inherent in the internal life of any organization but that the IBP's effectiveness would be diluted if they were brought outside its governing body, diminishing its prestige with lawyers and the public; expelling a governor who insisted on publicizing his disagreement with a duly approved policy was therefore a legal cause.

On the fourth issue, removal from the board ipso facto removed him as EVP, and the board's own rules and bylaws governed the filling of the vacancies; under Section 47 of Article VII the EVP automatically becomes president for the next succeeding term, which implied that the successor had to come from the 2003-2005 board.

Bar Matter 491 was read to mean that it is the EVP position that is rotated among the nine regional governors, the rotation of the presidency being merely a consequence of automatic succession -- and the bylaws' intrinsic principle is that whoever assumes the highest position must first have been exposed to the demands of national leadership.

stances.claim: A judgment of suspension against a Filipino lawyer in a foreign jurisdiction transmutes into a similar judgment here only if the basis of the foreign court's action included a ground for disbarment or suspension in our jurisdiction.
stances.rhetorical_move: applying a named precedent, Maquera, as the gateway rule before examining the foreign record at all

stances.claim: By depositing his client's $12,000 check in his own bank account and using it for his own benefit, de Vera was guilty of malpractice, gross misconduct and unethical behavior, violating his oath to conduct himself with all good fidelity to his client -- yet because a lesser penalty could accomplish the end desired, suspension for two years, not disbarment, was the appropriate sanction.
stances.rhetorical_move: treating the lawyer's own defense of authorization as an implied admission, then tempering the sanction by proportionality to the amount involved

stances.claim: Transferring chapter membership in order to become eligible for the IBP national presidency is not unethical: neither the Code of Professional Responsibility nor the Lawyer's Oath punishes lawyers for aspiring to that office or forbids them from doing perfectly legal acts to accomplish that goal.
stances.rhetorical_move: refusing to read an ethical prohibition into silence, separating ambition from misconduct

stances.claim: The position of IBP executive vice-president is not property in the constitutional sense and carries no security of tenure, and due process in administrative proceedings is satisfied by the opportunity to explain one's side -- an opportunity de Vera had, since he received the Complaint, was present at the meeting and answered his accuser on the record.
stances.rhetorical_move: narrowing the constitutional guarantee to its object (life, liberty, property) and then showing the record supplied what process was due

stances.claim: Expelling a governor who insisted on bringing his disagreement with a duly approved board resolution before the public was a legal cause for removal, because an organization's effectiveness is diluted when its internal conflicts are aired outside its governing body.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional-cohesion rationale, weighing the group's authority to speak for its members against an individual's public dissent

stances.claim: The rotation rule pertains to the office of executive vice-president while the presidency passes by automatic succession, so the replacement EVP had to be drawn from the 2003-2005 board -- making the elections of Governor Santiago and then Governor Salazar valid exercises of the board's authority under its bylaws.
stances.rhetorical_move: close reading of the phrase 'for the next succeeding term', supported by the bylaws' intrinsic principle of prior national leadership experience

notable_anecdotes: The disciplinary case reached back to a 1986 automobile accident in California: a $12,000 settlement check received for a client named Julius Wills III was deposited in the lawyer's personal account, and the California proceeding ended not in judgment but in his resignation from that bar.
The quarrel that cost him his IBP offices began over a withdrawn Petition against the Senate, which he attacked in the plenary session of the 10th National IBP Convention.
The removal moved with unusual speed: Governor Rivera wrote on May 12, 2005, and the board voted him out of both his posts the very next day at its 20th regular meeting.

The succession changed hands twice in twelve days -- Governor Santiago was elected EVP on June 13, relinquished the position voluntarily on June 20, and Governor Salazar was elected on June 25 at the board's last regular meeting.
Even while his removal was pending, de Vera had written the Court asking it to schedule his oath-taking as IBP national president, the request that became Bar Matter No. 1227.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 29 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Velez v. De Vera, a per curiam ruling consolidating a disciplinary complaint with two companion matters over the succession to the presidency of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines. Zoilo Antonio Velez sought Atty. Leonard de Vera's suspension or disbarment for concealing a California suspension order and for circumventing the rotation rule by transferring his chapter membership to Agusan del Sur; meanwhile the IBP board, after de Vera publicly attacked its withdrawal of a Petition against the Senate at the 10th National Convention, voted on May 13, 2005 by two thirds of its remaining members to remove him as governor and executive vice-president, and then elected Governor Santiago and, after she relinquished the post, Governor Salazar as EVP. The Court held first that an earlier case on his qualification to run as governor was no bar to the present complaint, since the two differed in subject matter, cause of action and relief. On the merits, citing Maquera, it held that a foreign suspension transmutes into a Philippine one only if its basis is also a ground here, and found that by insisting he had been authorized to use his client's money de Vera impliedly admitted using the $12,000 settlement check he had deposited in his own account -- conduct indicative of lack of integrity and propriety and amounting to malpractice, gross misconduct and unethical behavior. Because a lesser penalty could accomplish the end desired, it imposed suspension for two years rather than disbarment, while holding that his transfer of chapter membership was within his rights, since nothing punishes a lawyer for aspiring to the IBP presidency. It upheld his removal, ruling that the EVP position is not property in the constitutional sense and carries no security of tenure, that due process in administrative proceedings is simply the opportunity to explain one's side, which the record showed he had, and that publicizing his disagreement with a duly approved resolution was legal cause because an organization's effectiveness is diluted when internal conflicts are brought outside its governing body. Finally, reading Bar Matter 491 and the bylaws together, it held that the rotation rule attaches to the EVP office while the presidency passes by automatic succession, so the replacement had to come from the 2003-2005 board, and the elections of Santiago and Salazar were valid.
